blocks.en: The Road to Jerusalem: Grace and the Greater Sign
blocks.es_reference: El camino a Jerusalén: la gracia y la señal mayor

blocks.en: Setting His Face to Jerusalem, the Parables of Grace, and the Raising of Lazarus
blocks.es_reference: Afirmar el rostro hacia Jerusalén, las parábolas de la gracia y la resurrección de Lázaro

blocks.en: 1. He Set His Face to Jerusalem
blocks.es_reference: 1. Afirmó su rostro hacia Jerusalén

blocks.en: The turning point of Unit 5 now becomes a journey. Luke marks it with a solemn sentence: "when the time had come for Him to be received up, He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51). He did not drift toward the cross; He walked toward it with open eyes, deliberately, knowing what waited. From here the long road of Luke's travel narrative unfolds, and along it Jesus teaches the heart of the gospel.
blocks.es_reference: El punto de giro de la Unidad 5 ahora se vuelve un viaje. Lucas lo marca con una frase solemne: “cuando se cumplió el tiempo en que había de ser recibido arriba, afirmó su rostro para ir a Jerusalén” (Lucas 9:51). No fue a la deriva hacia la cruz; caminó hacia ella con los ojos abiertos, deliberadamente, sabiendo lo que le esperaba. Desde aquí se despliega el largo camino del relato del viaje de Lucas, y por él Jesús enseña el corazón del evangelio.

blocks.en: He also made plain that this road is no easy one. To a man who said he would follow Him anywhere, Jesus answered, "Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head" (Luke 9:58). To another He said, "Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and preach the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:60). And to a third: "No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:62). To follow the One who is going to a cross is no light thing; it asks the whole man, and it does not look back.
blocks.es_reference: También dejó claro que este camino no es fácil. A uno que dijo que le seguiría a dondequiera, Jesús respondió: “Las zorras tienen guaridas, y las aves de los cielos nidos; mas el Hijo del Hombre no tiene dónde recostar su cabeza” (Lucas 9:58). A otro le dijo: “Deja que los muertos entierren a sus muertos; y tú ve, anuncia el reino de Dios” (Lucas 9:60). Y a un tercero: “Ninguno que poniendo su mano en el arado mira hacia atrás, es apto para el reino de Dios” (Lucas 9:62). Seguir al que va a una cruz no es cosa ligera; pide al hombre entero, y no mira atrás.

blocks.en: The journey's very first step taught mercy. A Samaritan village would not receive Him, and James and John wanted to call down fire from heaven to consume it; but He turned and rebuked them, for the Son of Man "did not come to destroy men's lives but to save them" (Luke 9:55–56). The road to the cross is paved with mercy, not vengeance.
blocks.es_reference: El primer paso mismo del viaje enseñó misericordia. Una aldea de samaritanos no quiso recibirle, y Jacobo y Juan querían hacer descender fuego del cielo para consumirla; pero Él se volvió y los reprendió, porque el Hijo del Hombre “no ha venido para perder las almas de los hombres, sino para salvarlas” (Lucas 9:55–56). El camino a la cruz está empedrado de misericordia, no de venganza.

blocks.en: 2. Who Is My Neighbor? The Good Samaritan
blocks.es_reference: 2. ¿Quién es mi prójimo? El buen samaritano

blocks.en: A lawyer stood up to test Him: "Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" (Luke 10:25). Jesus turned him to the law, and the man recited it well — love God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself. But then, "wanting to justify himself," he asked, "And who is my neighbor?" (Luke 10:29). It is the question of a man looking for the edge of his duty — how few may I love and still be safe?
blocks.es_reference: Un intérprete de la ley se levantó para probarle: “Maestro, ¿haciendo qué cosa heredaré la vida eterna?” (Lucas 10:25). Jesús lo remitió a la ley, y el hombre la recitó bien — amar a Dios con todo el corazón, y al prójimo como a sí mismo. Pero entonces, “queriendo justificarse a sí mismo,” preguntó: “¿Y quién es mi prójimo?” (Lucas 10:29). Es la pregunta de quien busca el límite de su deber — ¿a cuán pocos puedo amar y aún estar a salvo?

blocks.en: So Jesus told of a man beaten by robbers and left half dead on the Jericho road. A priest saw him and passed by on the other side; a Levite did the same. Then a Samaritan — the despised half-breed, the very last man a Jewish lawyer would have chosen — came, "and when he saw him, he had compassion" (Luke 10:33). He bound the wounds, carried the man to an inn, and paid for his care. Then Jesus turned the lawyer's question inside out. The man had asked, "Who is my neighbor?" — whom am I obliged to love? Jesus asked instead, "Which of these three do you think was neighbor to him who fell among the thieves?" (Luke 10:36). The answer could only be, "He who showed mercy." — "Go and do likewise" (Luke 10:37). Do not ask who qualifies as your neighbor; be a neighbor, and let your mercy cross every line, as the Samaritan crossed the deepest line of all.
blocks.es_reference: Así que Jesús habló de un hombre asaltado por ladrones y dejado medio muerto en el camino de Jericó. Un sacerdote lo vio y pasó de largo por el otro lado; un levita hizo lo mismo. Entonces un samaritano — el mestizo despreciado, el último hombre que un intérprete judío habría escogido — vino, “y viéndole, fue movido a misericordia” (Lucas 10:33). Vendó sus heridas, lo llevó a un mesón y pagó su cuidado. Luego Jesús volvió la pregunta del revés. El hombre había preguntado: “¿Quién es mi prójimo?” — ¿a quién estoy obligado a amar? Jesús preguntó en cambio: “¿Quién, pues, de estos tres te parece que fue el prójimo del que cayó en manos de los ladrones?” (Lucas 10:36). La respuesta solo podía ser: “El que usó de misericordia.” — “Ve, y haz tú lo mismo” (Lucas 10:37). No preguntes quién califica como tu prójimo; sé un prójimo, y deja que tu misericordia cruce toda línea, como el samaritano cruzó la más honda de todas.

blocks.en: Yet love for the neighbor must spring from love for the Lord. In the very next scene Martha was "distracted with much serving" while her sister Mary sat at Jesus' feet to hear His word. Martha complained, but Jesus answered, "Martha, Martha, you are worried and troubled about many things. But one thing is needed," and said Mary had chosen "that good part, which will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:41–42). The mercy of the Samaritan and the stillness of Mary belong together: true service flows from sitting at the feet of Jesus.
blocks.es_reference: Sin embargo, el amor al prójimo debe brotar del amor al Señor. En la escena siguiente Marta estaba “distraída con muchos quehaceres” mientras su hermana María se sentaba a los pies de Jesús a oír su palabra. Marta se quejó, pero Jesús respondió: “Marta, Marta, afanada y turbada estás con muchas cosas; pero una cosa es necesaria,” y dijo que María había escogido “la buena parte, la cual no le será quitada” (Lucas 10:41–42). La misericordia del samaritano y la quietud de María van juntas: el verdadero servicio brota de sentarse a los pies de Jesús.

blocks.en: 3. Lost and Found: The Heart of Grace
blocks.es_reference: 3. Perdido y hallado: el corazón de la gracia

blocks.en: The Pharisees grumbled: "This Man receives sinners and eats with them" (Luke 15:2). In answer Jesus told three parables of the lost being found. A shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one lost sheep "until he finds it," and comes home rejoicing (Luke 15:4–6). A woman sweeps the house and searches until she finds her one lost coin, and calls her friends to rejoice (Luke 15:8–9). And the point of both: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents" (Luke 15:10).
blocks.es_reference: Los fariseos murmuraban: “Este a los pecadores recibe, y con ellos come” (Lucas 15:2). En respuesta, Jesús contó tres parábolas de lo perdido que es hallado. Un pastor deja las noventa y nueve y va tras la oveja perdida “hasta encontrarla,” y vuelve gozoso (Lucas 15:4–6). Una mujer barre la casa y busca hasta hallar su moneda perdida, y llama a sus amigas para gozarse (Lucas 15:8–9). Y el punto de ambas: “hay gozo delante de los ángeles de Dios por un pecador que se arrepiente” (Lucas 15:10).

blocks.en: Then comes the crown of the three. A younger son demanded his inheritance, went to a far country, and wasted it all, until he was feeding pigs and longing for their food. "But when he came to himself" (Luke 15:17) he resolved, "I will arise and go to my father," rehearsing his confession. And here the parable breaks every expectation: "when he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and fell on his neck and kissed him" (Luke 15:20). In that world a grown man of standing did not run; the father's running is undignified, scandalous grace. Before the boy could finish his speech the father called for the best robe, a ring, sandals, the fatted calf — not a hired servant's place, but a son's. Grace does not wait at the door with folded arms; it runs to meet the returning sinner.
blocks.es_reference: Luego viene la corona de las tres. Un hijo menor exigió su herencia, se fue a una provincia apartada y lo malgastó todo, hasta que apacentaba cerdos y anhelaba su comida. “Y volviendo en sí” (Lucas 15:17), resolvió: “Me levantaré e iré a mi padre,” ensayando su confesión. Y aquí la parábola rompe toda expectativa: “cuando aún estaba lejos, lo vio su padre, y fue movido a misericordia, y corrió, y se echó sobre su cuello, y le besó” (Lucas 15:20). En aquel mundo un hombre adulto de posición no corría; el correr del padre es gracia indigna, escandalosa. Antes de que el muchacho terminara su discurso, el padre mandó traer el mejor vestido, un anillo, calzado, el becerro gordo — no el lugar de un jornalero, sino el de un hijo. La gracia no espera en la puerta con los brazos cruzados; corre al encuentro del pecador que vuelve.

blocks.en: But the story does not end there. The elder brother, dutiful and cold, refused to go in: "these many years I have been serving you... yet you never gave me a young goat" (Luke 15:29). He had stayed home and still missed the father's heart, resenting the grace shown to his brother. He is the grumbling Pharisee, and the parable is left open — the father pleads with him, but we never learn whether he came in. The same heart appears in another parable: a Pharisee thanked God he was not like other men, while a tax collector beat his breast and cried, "God, be merciful to me a sinner!" Jesus said this man went home justified rather than the other, "for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted" (Luke 18:13–14).
blocks.es_reference: Pero la historia no termina ahí. El hermano mayor, cumplidor y frío, no quiso entrar: “He aquí, tantos años te sirvo... y nunca me has dado un cabrito” (Lucas 15:29). Se había quedado en casa y aun así perdió el corazón del padre, resintiendo la gracia mostrada a su hermano. Es el fariseo que murmura, y la parábola queda abierta — el padre le ruega, pero nunca sabemos si entró. El mismo corazón aparece en otra parábola: un fariseo daba gracias a Dios de no ser como los demás, mientras un publicano se golpeaba el pecho y clamaba: “Dios, sé propicio a mí, pecador.” Jesús dijo que este descendió justificado antes que el otro, “porque cualquiera que se enaltece, será humillado; y el que se humilla, será enaltecido” (Lucas 18:13–14).

blocks.en: 4. I Am the Resurrection and the Life
blocks.es_reference: 4. Yo soy la resurrección y la vida

blocks.en: Then, in Bethany, came the greatest sign of all. Lazarus, whom Jesus loved, fell sick; yet when word came, Jesus stayed two more days where He was (John 11:6), so that by the time He arrived Lazarus had been four days dead. Martha met Him: "Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died." Jesus answered with the fifth great I AM: "I am the resurrection and the life. He who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live" (John 11:25). He does not merely grant resurrection; He is it. Martha answered with her own confession: "Yes, Lord, I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God" (John 11:27). He had let Lazarus die on purpose, He told the disciples, "that you may believe" (John 11:15); and at the tomb He reminded Martha, "Did I not say to you that if you would believe you would see the glory of God?" (John 11:40).
blocks.es_reference: Entonces, en Betania, vino la mayor señal de todas. Lázaro, a quien Jesús amaba, enfermó; pero cuando llegó el aviso, Jesús se quedó dos días más donde estaba (Juan 11:6), de modo que al llegar, Lázaro llevaba cuatro días muerto. Marta salió a su encuentro: “Señor, si hubieses estado aquí, mi hermano no habría muerto.” Jesús respondió con el quinto gran YO SOY: “Yo soy la resurrección y la vida; el que cree en mí, aunque esté muerto, vivirá” (Juan 11:25). No solo concede la resurrección; Él es la resurrección. Marta respondió con su propia confesión: “Sí, Señor; yo he creído que tú eres el Cristo, el Hijo de Dios” (Juan 11:27). Había dejado morir a Lázaro a propósito, dijo a los discípulos, “para que creáis” (Juan 11:15); y junto al sepulcro recordó a Marta: “¿No te he dicho que si crees, verás la gloria de Dios?” (Juan 11:40).

blocks.en: At the tomb came the shortest verse in Scripture: "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). He knew He would raise Lazarus within the hour, and still He wept — real tears at a real grave. As God He is the resurrection; as man He weeps with the grieving. Then He cried with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come forth!" (John 11:43), and the dead man came out, still bound in his graveclothes. "Loose him, and let him go."
blocks.es_reference: Junto al sepulcro vino el versículo más corto de la Escritura: “Jesús lloró” (Juan 11:35). Sabía que levantaría a Lázaro dentro de una hora, y aun así lloró — lágrimas reales ante una tumba real. Como Dios es la resurrección; como hombre llora con los que lloran. Entonces clamó a gran voz: “¡Lázaro, ven fuera!” (Juan 11:43), y el muerto salió, aún atado en sus vendas. “Desatadle, y dejadle ir.”

blocks.en: And here is the terrible irony. Many who saw it believed; but the chief priests and Pharisees, more alarmed than ever, "plotted from that day on to put Him to death" (John 11:53) — and even planned to kill Lazarus too (John 12:10). The greatest sign of life became the trigger of the plot of death. The One who raises the dead walked on, steadily, toward His own grave.
blocks.es_reference: Y aquí está la ironía terrible. Muchos que lo vieron creyeron; pero los principales sacerdotes y los fariseos, más alarmados que nunca, “desde aquel día acordaron matarle” (Juan 11:53) — y aun pensaron matar también a Lázaro (Juan 12:10). La mayor señal de vida se volvió el detonante del complot de muerte. El que levanta a los muertos siguió caminando, firme, hacia su propia tumba.

blocks.en: 5. The Heart of God on the Road to a Cross
blocks.es_reference: 5. El corazón de Dios camino de una cruz

blocks.en: The road to Jerusalem reveals two things at once. It shows the heart of God — a grace that seeks the lost sheep, sweeps for the lost coin, and runs down the road to a returning son, and that justifies the tax collector who cries for mercy. And it shows the power of the Son — the resurrection and the life, who calls the dead from the tomb. Both press straight toward the cross: the grace will be bought there, and the sign of Lazarus's life will seal the decision to kill Him.
blocks.es_reference: El camino a Jerusalén revela dos cosas a la vez. Muestra el corazón de Dios — una gracia que busca la oveja perdida, barre por la moneda perdida y corre camino abajo hacia el hijo que vuelve, y que justifica al publicano que clama por misericordia. Y muestra el poder del Hijo — la resurrección y la vida, que llama a los muertos de la tumba. Ambas cosas empujan derecho hacia la cruz: la gracia será comprada allí, y la señal de la vida de Lázaro sellará la decisión de matarle.

blocks.en: And the divine/human pattern stands plain. He who is the resurrection wept at a grave; He who receives sinners set His face to die for them. So the road asks of us what it asked then: come home like the prodigal, cry for mercy like the tax collector, and believe in the One who is the resurrection and the life. The road runs toward a grave, but it is the road of life.
blocks.es_reference: Y el patrón divino/humano está claro. El que es la resurrección lloró ante una tumba; el que recibe a los pecadores puso su rostro para morir por ellos. Así que el camino nos pide lo que pidió entonces: vuelve a casa como el hijo pródigo, clama por misericordia como el publicano, y cree en el que es la resurrección y la vida. El camino lleva a una tumba, pero es el camino de la vida.

sa.prompt: Explain “He set His face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51) and what Jesus taught about the cost of following.
sa.model: Luke says that when the time came, Jesus steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem. He did not drift toward the cross but walked toward it deliberately, knowing what waited. He also taught that following Him is costly: the Son of Man had nowhere to lay His head, and no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom. The journey to the cross asks the whole person.

sa.prompt: Retell the parable of the Good Samaritan and explain how Jesus reframed the lawyer's question (Luke 10:25-37).
sa.model: A lawyer, wanting to justify himself, asked “who is my neighbor?” Jesus told of a man left half dead, passed by a priest and a Levite, but helped by a despised Samaritan who had compassion, bound his wounds, and paid for his care. Then Jesus reframed the question: not “who is my neighbor?” but “which one proved to be a neighbor?” The answer was the one who showed mercy. “Go and do likewise.”

sa.prompt: What does the scene of Mary and Martha (Luke 10:38-42) teach about the one needful thing?
sa.model: While Martha was distracted with much serving, her sister Mary sat at Jesus' feet to hear His word. When Martha complained, Jesus said she was worried about many things, but one thing is needed, and Mary had chosen the good part, which would not be taken from her. Love for the neighbor must spring from love for the Lord; true service flows from sitting at His feet.

sa.prompt: Explain the heart of grace in the lost sheep, lost coin, and prodigal son (Luke 15).
sa.model: When the Pharisees grumbled that He received sinners, Jesus told of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the prodigal son, all sought and found with joy. The crown is the father who, while the son was still far off, ran and fell on his neck and kissed him, restoring him as a son with robe, ring, and feast. Grace does not wait at the door; it runs to meet the returning sinner.

sa.prompt: What do the elder brother and the Pharisee-and-tax-collector teach about self-righteousness and mercy?
sa.model: The elder brother, dutiful and cold, refused to go in and resented the grace shown to his brother; he pictures the grumbling Pharisees, near the father's house but far from his heart. The same heart appears in the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like others, while the tax collector beat his breast and cried for mercy. Jesus said the tax collector, not the Pharisee, went home justified, for whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

sa.prompt: What did Jesus claim to Martha in “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25-27)?
sa.model: When Lazarus died, Martha said if Jesus had been there her brother would not have died. Jesus answered, “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in Me, though he may die, he shall live.” He does not merely grant resurrection — He is it. Martha confessed He is the Christ, the Son of God. The claim and her faith meet at the grave.

sa.prompt: Explain “Jesus wept” and “Lazarus, come forth” — the divine/human pattern at the tomb (John 11:35-44).
sa.model: At the tomb Jesus wept, the shortest verse in Scripture, though He knew He would raise Lazarus within the hour — real tears at a real grave. As God He is the resurrection; as man He weeps with the grieving. Then He cried, “Lazarus, come forth!” and the dead man came out, still bound, and Jesus said, “Loose him, and let him go.”

sa.prompt: Explain the irony of the raising of Lazarus (John 11:45-53; 12:10).
sa.model: Raising Lazarus was the greatest sign, and many who saw it believed. But the chief priests and Pharisees, more alarmed than ever, plotted from that day to put Jesus to death, and even planned to kill Lazarus. The greatest sign of life became the trigger of the plot of death. The One who raises the dead walked on toward His own grave.

sa.prompt: What two things does the road to Jerusalem reveal (the heart of God and the power of the Son)?
sa.model: The road to Jerusalem reveals two things at once: the heart of God in a grace that seeks the lost sheep, runs to the prodigal, and justifies the humble; and the power of the Son, the resurrection and the life who calls the dead from the tomb. Both press toward the cross, where grace is bought and where the sign of Lazarus seals the plot to kill Him.

sa.prompt: What does the road to Jerusalem ask of us?
sa.model: The road to Jerusalem asks of us what it asked then. We are to come home like the prodigal son, cry for mercy like the tax collector rather than boast like the Pharisee, and believe in the One who is the resurrection and the life. As God He wept at a grave; as man He set His face to die for sinners. The road runs toward a grave, but it is the road of life.
